utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones appearing on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant Ms. Jasmina Cosic and Ms. Adisa Mehic, attending today for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and welcome back. I hope you're feeling better. So good afternoon to you and your team, of course. Any preliminaries before we bring in this witness? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Last Friday we filed a -- we filed and sent to the parties a new schedule for witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- including and referring to videolink witness in that respect we filed also an addendum to a prior filed motion. And I contacted Defence counsel in that respect and requested them for any cooperation, if possible, to respond on short term and they told me to do so. So I'm much obliged in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have another issue. That's related, Your Honour, to that issue we already addressed last week about sending of proofing notes and in exhibit list prior to the witness itself. Yesterday my case manager received from legal assistant an e-mail, legal assistant of the Defence team and, in that e-mail, there is a reference to the witness projected now for today and that's okay, of course, when on the level of case manager versus case manager of the other team there is an exchange on information. Well, in this e-mail of yesterday, there is also reference to general issues of policy of disclosure and a kind of representing the team, the Defence team referring to "we are sending you this message" and there is a request to the OTP not to delay any disclosure for any witness and also reference to a language like "we will vigorously seek adjournments" and the practice of late disclosure. Well, in my opinion, that's not true at all, but at the same time, I noticed that a message is sent to our case manager and not to me as lead counsel. So in that respect, there should be a better practice for exchanging such information and not by legal assistant and also copying to other parties. Then excluding me as the lead counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Let's take them one by one. I want to make sure that I have understood you well. This addendum to the Prosecution motion for the testimony of a witness via video-conference link, do I take it that you are informing the Trial Chamber that the Defence has agreed that there would be a video-conference testimony on the 4th and 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was that I -- I was seeking cooperation that I would file an early response to it, rather than to wait for 14 days and it had been confirmed that they will do their best and today or tomorrow they will try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So I was understanding well. Yes, Mr. Jones, what's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct firstly that we indicated we would respond promptly and, in fact, the position is that we won't oppose the Prosecution motion. We won't actually file anything but we won't oppose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. So here and now we can grant the motion and in other words there will be video-link conference for the purposes of this addendum and the original motion video conference link would be as requested, that is on the 4th and on the 5th of April of 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's sorted out. Do you require -- I don't think you do require a written one for the purpose of just the videolink? I don't think so. Anyway, if you need a written one, we will provide you with a written one but I think an oral decision would suffice. I don't know. I mean I have signed others before, of course, but I honestly don't remember whether it's requisite or whether we can do with --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I don't remember requisite, Your Honour, but I know that it's not only the mission for OTP involved but also for registry and other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is why I'm saying whether you require a written decision, written order. I don't think so. If you require one, we'll have one put in place in five minutes. Trial Chamber two is very efficient. Yes, the second matter. Please, I invite you both not to take much of the Chamber's time on this matter. You know what I have stated earlier. This is more of a matter of courtesy to start with, a matter of keeping each one another informed. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I could probably respond in about ten seconds. As far as e-mails are concerned, there's always a certain informality. I don't know how helpful it is to ventilate it before the Trial Chamber. But for the sake of clarity, I, in fact, drafted the text of that e-mail and sent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And the reasons -- the reasons for why that was a convenient way of dealing with matters. It was really the message seemed to be more important than the message be better -- be gotten across that we didn't want any delays rather than how the message was sent. Having said that, the point is taken. Obviously when the lead counsel was away, there might have been certain irregular communications if I can put it that way and we're happy to keep -- lead counsel to lead counsel communications in the spirit that Mr. Wubben asks for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. But again, I enjoin you these matters can be sorted out between you or amongst you in the most amicable manner. Plus the use of certain words is normal legal parlance in the tradition, for example, that I am used to, like we will vigorously seek adjournments. This is something that -- this is how we talk or how we speak. So don't take it as if it's meant to send out loud and clear war-like messages. I mean, this is how we talk. So don't worry about it Mr. Wubben. I mean, I would suggest that you try to do -- you know, find a common ground amongst you without involving the Tribunal -- the Trial Chamber as much as you can, in these matters. Because I'm sure that there is always a solution. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I hope that I don't have to address your Trial Chamber when this happen again. I will seek to try to prevent this and contact Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is the best way to go about it and then we will see if there are problems obviously. Anything else before we bring in the witness? No. You have had now the proofing notes and all the documents that you needed?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we pretty much have everything. There are one or two matters still to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next thing because forewarned is forearmed. This gentleman, who will be joining us soon to give testimony has given lengthy statements to the office of the -- obviously, with practically all the cases involved in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in mind. I mean this statement covers not just this case, but covers a lot of other cases. So please try to restrict your examination-in-chief and your cross-examination to what is relevant to this case. MR. DI FAZIO: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise we would be opening a far wider horizon than we actually need. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. There is no question that I -- I will be as selective as I can. But just from what Your Honours say, I wonder that I -- I hope that you have all the material. I know that you got the statements beforehand. You have a statement, I think, dated September/July 2001 and another one dated -- and March 2002, it's a big one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Going to 36 pages you have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Is that all you have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Then we have another one which is dated -- 21st of September 2002 and first and second of November 2002. So that's -- and we have them in both language. MR. DI FAZIO: The statements aren't going to be gone through chapter and verse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope not. This is why I'm making myself clear. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand what Your Honours want and that will not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are topics -- subject matter that is very tempting both Prosecution and Defence, to -- MR. DI FAZIO: There will be a little bit of background but only to help you understand subsequent actions in the all important month of March in Srebrenica. That's the context in which that would be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The information on how UNPROFOR came about, it's -- there is a lot of information that we don't need for this case. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not going to go into that chapter and verse. There is just one or two points I need to make about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's start. Where is the witness? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. Pretty soon you're going to start giving evidence in this case, which has been instituted by the Prosecution against Naser Oric. I take it that you are familiar with the court proceedings. Our rules require that before you start giving evidence, you address a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is going to be handed to you by Madam Usher. Please go ahead and read it and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think I need to explain to you the procedure. Mr. Di Fazio will go first for the Prosecution. How long do you expect your examination-in-chief to be, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two days, all right. And Mr. Jones, another two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I think a day and a half anyway, five hours, five to six hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm telling you this because however much I tried to find some time while we are not sitting, I have another initial appearance this week, another new comer, which again has also been assigned to my chamber and I will need to have the initial appearance on Thursday. Now, my senior legal officer is doing his level best to arrange it so that as soon as we start a break here on Thursday afternoon, I move to another courtroom and start with the initial appearance and try to get it over and done as quick -- as quickly as possible. But there are, I think, 20 counts, so that will take time. I mean this morning I had 37 counts and it took me an hour and a half. So that will take an hour at least, an hour, hour and a quarter or less because there is only one accused. It will take me 45 minutes to an hour. Which basically means that we might have to lose about 30 minutes from our case on Thursday. All right. So as we go along, please try to make your assessment as to where we stand and decide whether we need to have another witness here -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- on Friday or not. All right. It's your assessment. I will stay by it, in other words, I will cooperate with you, of course, and this is an important witness. Information he is going to give us is very important, fundamental to the case, and I will allow you all the time that you need, both of you, to examine and cross-examine this witness as you wish, as you desire, as you need. All right. Which basically means, Mr. Tucker, that you may get stuck here in The Hague for the next few days or until the end of the week. I know I can count on your full cooperation. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, please go ahead. Examined by Mr. Di Fazio: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I think you still have a commission in the British army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'll refer to you as Colonel Tucker. I just want to go through some background material. You were educated in the United Kingdom, attended University in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You graduated summa cum laude in mechanical engineering?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you graduate, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that, had you attended the Royal Military Academy in Sandhurst between 1976 and 1977?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a commissioned officer in the royal artillery?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have qualified as an artillery forward observer?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A troop commander?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a battery commander?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have therefore had experience in leading and commanding men, as a troop commander and battery commander?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both tasks place differing numbers of men under your command, I believe, about fifty as a troop commander?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about 200 men as a battery commander?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You attended the junior division of the staff college in 1976?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just briefly explain what the junior division of the staff college is, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It's a course for captains in the British army to prepare them for company command and company second in command and it covers administrative duties and staff duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And you graduated top out of 130 students there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also attended the German general staff college between 1989 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you there came 3rd out of 60 students undergoing that course?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've seen service in Northern Ireland on three occasions where you worked as an intelligence officer, a troop commander, battery commander and where you also received infantry training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between May and October of 1992, you were the military assistant to the chief of staff of NATO's headquarters, northern army group.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In October of 1992, you were posted as the military assistant to the commander of the United Nations Protection Force or UNPROFOR at their Bosnia-Herzegovina headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. I was posted as the military advisor to the commander of UNPROFOR's Bosnia-Herzegovina commands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Not of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, I see. Thank you very much for clarifying that. I'm going to return to that period of your work in due course. Following that, you performed a two-year service in Germany working as a battery commander with the British army?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: December 1995 to February 1996, you performed duties as a commander of a self-propelled-artillery battery in the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between June 1996 and December 1997 you led the Bosnia crisis management team in the UK, United Kingdom national crisis management headquarters which amongst other things was providing logistic support for the United Kingdom contingent of SFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left the British army in early 1998 and you basically have been working in the private sector since that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn -- ask you to turn your attention to UNPROFOR. I think that was established in March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I understand so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Was its mandate initially to monitor the cease-fire that was in place in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it based?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The forces of the -- of UNPROFOR were based obviously in Croatia in the UNPAs, whereas the headquarters for UNPROFOR was based in Sarajevo which at that time was thought to be a convenient logistic location that was not involved with any of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the deputy force commander?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet General Morillon and form a working relationship with him through 1992 and into 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a -- it's agreed there was an outbreak of hostilities in April of 1992 in Bosnia and did that cause UNPROFOR to pull out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, that made the management of -- and administration of UNPROFOR's headquarters in Sarajevo untenable and their ability to command and control the operations in Croatia and in the UNPAs impractical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In June of 1992, was the sector Sarajevo set up?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. Sector Sarajevo was set up. It was initially a Canadian battle group and then subsequently a Ukrainian and an Egyptian battalion were added.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many men did that number?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Combat soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did it have its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Its headquarters was in the PTT building in Sarajevo, halfway between the centre of Sarajevo and the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In September of 1992, was a decision taken to establish a new Bosnia-Herzegovina command?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. A command of what precisely, just explain the structure that was created.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: As we've just discussed, sector Sarajevo was the only UN forces in Bosnia. There had been a conference in London -- the London conference in August at which a number of nations had agreed that they would contribute troops in Bosnia in order to try and provide humanitarian aid and to facilitate cease-fires. The countries which had already provided troops, in other words, sector Sarajevo, remained and additional troops from the UK, from France, from Spain, Denmark, et cetera, about ten countries in total were put -- were established and a new headquarters was formed, headquarters Bosnia-Herzegovina command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned two aspects of its mandate, the delivery of humanitarian aid in Bosnia and the negotiation of cease-fires. Did that remain, the mandate of this new structure that was created throughout 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. For the time that I was there, that was the basis of the security council resolutions of which quite a number were passed during the period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct to describe that as the two principal objectives of the command, delivery of humanitarian aid throughout Bosnia and the negotiation of cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I would describe it as facilitation of cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Facilitation of cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly pause between question and answer, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're both speaking English so we don't have the usual hesitation so perhaps if we slow it down a bit. Was the Bosnia-Herzegovina command subordinate to UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it was. General Nambiar, the commander in Zagreb was General Morillon's superior commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bosnia-Herzegovina command develop a deployment capability in or around September October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. The additional forces to sector Sarajevo were deployed into Bosnia during October and November of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive to take up your duties there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I arrived in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Morillon already there in Bosnia or did you join him? Or did he go with you to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. General Morillon was in Belgrade at that time. The route through which the forces not yet deployed in Bosnia, deployed into Bosnia was large -- was mostly through Belgrade. And so I met General Morillon in Belgrade and we then flew into Sarajevo towards the end of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you set up a command as a headquarter structure?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The headquarter structure that was set up was a small -- what I would describe as diplomatic elements inside Sarajevo in the residency building in Sarajevo, which had been Tito's summer residence and was about a kilometre north of the Presidency building in central Sarajevo. The remainder of the headquarters which was the bulk of the headquarters which was about 350 to 400 men was set up. It was established in a village called Kiseljak, which was about half an hour's drive outside of Sarajevo, away from Sarajevo in the direction -- in the direction of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Where did you and General Morillon work out of?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon established himself in the small diplomatic headquarters inside Sarajevo, whereas the military operations were directed from Kiseljak by General Morillon's chief of staff, Brigadier Cordy-Simpson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also worked out of the residency together with Morillon?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I worked with Morillon out of the residency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was the -- why was the -- why were the headquarters split in this way, with the bulk being at Kiseljak, the bulk of the working men being at Kiseljak and this smaller physical location within the residency in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The -- General Morillon believed it was very important to show international solidarity and recognition with the legally established government in Bosnia and -- however, that was inside a siege and encirclement and it would have been very difficult to carry out military operations, logistic operations from inside the siege. Therefore he decided that it would not be good military practice to constrain his operations by having them inside the siege.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kiseljak was effectively behind Muslim lines in Muslim hill territory?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was actually in the Croat -- the Bosnian Croat --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: -- part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks for clarifying that. What precisely were General Morillon's duties in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon carried out discussions, negotiations with the political and military leaders of all three factions who were engaged in hostilities inside Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that require or necessitate him travelling out of Sarajevo from time to time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you accompany him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I accompanied General Morillon wherever he went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that his duties involved carrying out discussions and negotiations with the political and military leaders of all three factions. And you've earlier referred to the mandate that the Bosnian headquarters had namely the facilitation of cease-fires and the facilitation, organisation of aid convoys. Were those two topics also his objectives? Was he trying to achieve that wherever possible?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That was the reason why he had meetings every day. Sometimes two, three meetings a day with various military and political leaders. And to explain the context, the prime task was the provision of humanitarian aid to those in need. Now, in order to achieve that, they could not be fighting or wherever there was fighting it prevented humanitarian aid to be delivered. So therefore getting cease-fires or arranging the facilitating of cease-fires was a necessary prerequisite to being able to deliver humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In carrying out his duties, did Morillon have to speak to local military commanders in order to facilitate -- help bring about a sort of cease-fires you have spoken of?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. All the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it important to him to ensure that he was in fact speaking to the - for want of a better word - real military commander in any particular area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it was essential and he became very angry when he was being delayed from speaking with the real commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. As -- in addition to speaking to military commanders, in order to facilitate cease-fires, did he have to speak to local politicians and also more powerful politicians in the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you assist him to set up these meetings, organise these meetings?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: My task was, firstly, to arrange the next day's meetings, the next week's meetings and that's to agree time, place, route, travel, agenda where relevant, and then secondly, to accompany the general, take notes during those meetings, then after the meeting, to draft General Morillon's reports about the meetings he had had during that day for approval by General Morillon for subsequent transmission to Zagreb to HQ UNPROFOR and specifically General Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The draft reports that you prepared on behalf of General Morillon, were they created using the notes that you have referred to? The notes that you took?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how long after an event, a meeting, a discussion, an occurrence, would you make these notes normally?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Most of my notes during meetings were made during the meeting itself. Taking notes as the conversation ebbed and flowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you were unable to do that, in other words, to take notes actually during a meeting or during an occurrence, how long after would you make notes?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Usually, at the latest, that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you made those notes at that time, were the events still fresh in your mind?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Unpleasantly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have in front of you a book. What is that book?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: This book is a diary. It's the diary that I wrote from the 10th of March, 1993 through to the 28th or 29th of March, 1993. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, I would like to show you that diary and the Defence that diary. I have a copy of it of course and it has the ERN number which has the advantage of having numbers on it and for the rest of this witness's evidence I would like, of course, to use the photocopied version which has the ERN, but I would like you to have an opportunity to just look at the notebook itself, the original, and perhaps if the usher could show it to the Defence. Also, to seek permission that the witness keep that original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Show it to the Defence first, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I would like also to seek permission that the witness keep that original. On occasions there has been marker pen used in it so the photocopy often sometimes doesn't pick up a date which the original, you will be able to see on the original. So if there is any problems, we can always have the -- refer to the original to see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the original -- let me see it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Before we proceed on this, Mr. Di Fazio, just a couple of questions. One to you and one to the witness. Of course, there will be absolutely no problem on our part that the witness will have this in front of him all the time while he is giving testimony. How do you intend to overcome the problem of making the witness refer to particular pages when this is not -- pages are not numbered in sequence, but the photocopy that you have has got sequential -- MR. DI FAZIO: By using the photocopy, but to have the original Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there in case there is some part of the photocopy that's not entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Because I think you will see blue marking pen. Blue doesn't come up well on photocopying. It obscures. Some photocopiers don't have that problem, but blue does. So that's all -- the witness will in fact refer to the photocopy so that we can all instantly go to a part of the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: It's just as back up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio and I am sure we will find a way. Also, just for the record, this now seems to have tags everywhere -- that are at least some of the blue are marked with a reference to the date, reference to dates. I don't see any of the red tags showing any markings on them. The question that I have to the witness -- for the witness is that, I came across two pages that seemed to have been torn off from this diary. Are you aware of this, to start with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation -- I mean, we just want to make sure that there is nothing fishy about it, that's what. It's your diary obviously and you can explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That diary was the only paper that I had in Srebrenica and I think we used them to light fires or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Usher, you could hand this back to the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, in light of the evidence of the -- evidence of Colonel Tucker, I seek to tender into evidence photocopies of this diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have, I take it, Mr. Jones, received a copy of this in good time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we have got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tucker, before we proceed or Colonel Tucker, this diary has never left your custody? You've always retained custody of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Has it been given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't asked. MR. DI FAZIO: I seek to tender it into evidence if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document being a diary kept by witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This diary being a photocopy of -- this document being a photocopy of a diary kept by witness Colonel Tucker and starting with ERN number 04193416 and ending with ERN number 04193608 is being tendered and received in evidence and marked Prosecution Exhibit P510. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, the general taskings of General Morillon and Bosnian headquarters was, I think, onerous and required you to focus on various aspects of the country at different times. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you prioritize your attention from week-to-week, month-to-month, in the period of time from October to March of 1993? How did you decide where to direct your energies, your efforts, your manpower?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The priority that General Morillon took was, firstly, any orders that he may have received from General Nambiar, of which he did not during that time. Secondly, it was to listen to what the Presidency, and by that I mean President Izetbegovic and his major interlocutor, Dr. Ganic, what they said and where they wished General Morillon to focus his attention. Secondly, on what the Bosnian Serb leadership, that's Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic, where they wished concern to be focussed and, thirdly, what the Croat authorities and the main person with whom General Morillon spoke in that context was with Brigadier General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the period of time between October and Christmas of 1992, where was the main -- what was the main focus of your attention?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The main focus before Christmas 1992 was the situation around Sarajevo and the siege and the utilities -- that's electricity, water, gas, and the plight of the population inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that period of time, did General Morillon have meetings with the Serb leadership, including General Mladic and Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. A whole series.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just said that the primary focus of attention for Bosnia command was Sarajevo. In that period of time, October to Christmas, 1992, did you have occasion to focus your attention and your energies on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we did and it wasn't just Srebrenica. It was also Gorazde. And what happened was that the prime focus was Sarajevo, but in the background there was an ongoing and continuous attempt by the United Nations to get humanitarian aid convoys into the Gorazde pocket and into the Srebrenica pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did, in fact, -- did you in fact succeed in organizing an aid convoy into Srebrenica in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we managed to get a convoy of humanitarian aid into Srebrenica at the end of November, 1992, which is about, I think it's 27th of -- 28th November, it actually arrived at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Brigadier Cordy-Simpson play a role in the organisation of aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Cordy-Simpson who was General Morillon's chief of staff, who was leading operations from Kiseljak was the main implementer of all of the organisation, the logistics, the administration, of humanitarian aid convoys throughout Bosnia, and particularly the ones to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how large that particular convoy was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I believe it was ten -- ten -- 10-ton trucks, out -- which came from the Belgian Dutch transport battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how many tons of supplies would that have been able to transport into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: About 100 tons, about ten tons per truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said that one of the ways in which you prioritized your taskings was according to the -- what the leadership of the warring factions mentioned to you, what they were concerned about. Did you receive any communications of more serious concerns about what was happening in Srebrenica in that latter part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The concern that -- during 1992 was that there were people -- there were many refugees in those areas, that they'd been cut off since about May 1992, April/May 1992 and there were a lot of starving people there and that it was winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your source of information to establish that, namely the fact that there was large numbers of refugees, starvation and the -- winter obviously you knew, but what was your source of information about those conditions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: From the Presidency themselves, in other words Dr. Ganic, President Izetbegovic, Zlatko Lagumdzija who was the Bosniak minister for refugee affairs, and we had information from our own convoy which had got into -- had reached Srebrenica in November. They had reported about the conditions and circumstances that they found there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what the -- the thrust of the report was that you received from the persons who travelled in with a convoy?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The description of the circumstances in Srebrenica was that the conditions were quite bad. There were a lot of refugees. There were a number who were starving or close to starving. It was very cold but that there were -- there were -- there was livestock still in some -- in some fields that there were some supplies, that conditions were bad, but there were other parts of Bosnia at that time where conditions were worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Bosnian Presidency ever express any concerns to you in that latter part of 1992 about fighting that was going on in the area or that might have been going on in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. Their concern was continually: People are hungry, people are starving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've testified that during this period you also had communications with the Serb leadership. Did the Serb leadership express any concerns to you about any aspect of affairs in eastern Bosnia, in particular the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The Serb leadership, the conversations we had with the Serb leadership were always at our request. The Serb leadership were not seeking conversation with us about that area. They had no issues with us about that area. We had issues with them, because they were stopping our convoys getting through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have occasion, in the latter part of 1992 -- when I say you I mean yourself and General Morillon and other officers working with you in Bosnia -- Bosnian headquarters -- did you have occasion to speak to the Serbs about those impediments to the convoys?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. On quite a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to resolve those matters, or not? Or is it the case that you only succeeded in facilitating and organizing that one convoy in November?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We had planned something like four or five convoys to Srebrenica and to Gorazde because they were planned together. It was one convoy to Gorazde. One convoy to Srebrenica. We planned four or five. We only managed to get one through, the one that I've just told you about earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that because of obstruction from the Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was from -- it was due to obstruction on the ground. In other words, roadblocks, not letting convoys pass or sending them the wrong direction, claiming that there was fighting going on and therefore the convoy could not get through claiming that local population were angry and didn't want to let the convoys pass. There were a hundred excuses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the course of these conversations that you had with the Serb leadership, did they ever express any concerns about the action of Muslim military forces acting from out -- inside the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. The Serb leadership never talked -- during that period did not talk about the hostile activities of fighting or combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn your attention now to early -- early 1993. Was there any change in the nature of complaints from either the Serb leadership or the Muslim leadership regarding activities in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, it's a very small thing about Muslim leadership. So far this witness has been talking about the Bosnian Presidency, by which I understood the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So perhaps we should speak to the words he used. MR. DI FAZIO: That's precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones is certainly right, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: You understand what we're talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is, is any -- any change in the nature of complaints coming from the Bosnian Presidency and the Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Requests from the Presidency for humanitarian aid for the enclaves, in other words Gorazde and Srebrenica, continued. There was no -- this is in January I'm talking about. However, in early February, 1993, we started getting complaints from the Bosnian Serb leadership about attacks out of the Srebrenica enclave, specifically from the Srebrenica enclave, not from the Gorazde enclave, and these were -- there were two types of complaints. There was a complaint, which is a bitter complaint which was about attacks on villages and Serb civilians and the numbers that they were quoting were between a thousand and 1360 -- is a number that sticks in my memory. Serb civilians which they alleged had been killed by the Bosniak forces inside Srebrenica. The second reason for complaint was that the -- they claimed that the Bosniak forces were attacking their lines of communication from Zvornik, down to Pale and down to around Sarajevo. In other words, these were military operations which were making it difficult for the Serbs to carry out their -- their own military operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By this stage, had you and General Morillon had some experience in trying to facilitate and assist in the negotiations of cease-fires in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we had been trying to negotiate cease-fires since we had arrived in -- in Bosnia. There was a recurring theme to cease fires, which was that the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted a cease-fire or cease-fires to cover all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in other words they wanted to consolidate their gain and consolidate what they had taken, whereas the Bosniak leadership declared that they wanted cease-fires. The reality of the way they behaved was that whenever they were under pressure militarily from the Serbs, they wanted local cease-fires, but then contrived to try and break those cease-fires and provoke the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The complaints of attacks from the Serbs to you only started in early 1993, I understand.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In February?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those attacks that the Serbs were alleging, were in breach of cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The Serbs maintained -- or complained that the Bosniaks always sought aid from the United Nations for cease-fires when things were going badly for them, but then broke those cease-fires when it suited them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In early -- or in the -- in the first two months of 1993, did the Serbs, the Serb leadership mention any events in relation to a place called Kravica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In the middle of February, specific complaints were made and Kravica was mentioned and, what I mean is that they had made complaints in general, saying that attacks had happened, villages had been burnt, civilians had been massacred, but without naming any names or places. Then in the middle of February, and I believe it was General Gvero who made specific reference to one particular incidence which he claimed took place on the Orthodox, the Greek-Orthodox Christmas and a village called Kravica had been sacked and burnt and the population killed. And for some reason, he was particularly incensed and particularly angry about that particular incidence over and above a number of others that he made reference to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to this sudden increase in Serb complaints regarding Muslim attacks, did you get any information via the press in relation to Muslim military activity emanating out from the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. What happened was that in early January, we read and were notified by HQ UNPROFOR in Zagreb that there were reports in the international media of an offensive from -- launched in eastern Bosnia and which there were a couple of reports which even talked of Bosniak soldiers having seized some territory across the Drina into Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just explain to the Trial Chamber why it was that you relied on or actually considered press reports rather than any other sources of intelligence or information regarding events in that area.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: At that time the United Nations and HQ Bosnia-Herzegovina command had no forces, had no personnel of its own in eastern Bosnia who were in a position to see for themselves what was actually happening there. At that time, we had to rely totally on what we were being told by the -- by the Presidency and Bosniak politicians and military by what we were being told by Serb politicians and military and what we were being told by UNHCR personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned the complaints from the Serb leadership that you started to hear in the early part of 1993. Did complaints emanate from the Bosnian Presidency, the Muslim Bosnian Presidency concerning military events in the area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The Presidency had, up until mid January, towards the end of January, been -- their requests were the same as they had been since October when we arrived in Bosnia, which were humanitarian aid. We want humanitarian aid there. From the end of January onwards that started changing, and they started complaining about attacks being made by the Bosnian Serbs against the Srebrenica enclave, and they -- so their requests changed from being for humanitarian aid only to being for humanitarian aid and everything from military action against the Serbs, cease-fires, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you -- can you give us any idea approximately when this added component to their complaints came about, when this was.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: This additional dimension to the -- to the requests, complaints from the Presidency started at the very end of January and then steadily intensified throughout February until it reached a crescendo in the beginning of March when President Izetbegovic personally asked General Morillon to go there in person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about that in particular. Firstly, were you present when this request was made by President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the request made?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was made in President Izetbegovic's office in the Presidency in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I assume General Morillon was present?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, General Morillon was present. President Izetbegovic was present. President Izetbegovic's interpreter was present. I was present and Mihailov, General Morillon's bodyguard was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just while we're there, just a bit more about Mihailov, who exactly was he?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Mihailov was a French foreign region sergeant major who was Macedonian by origin and spoke a fluent Serbo-Croat and he accompanied General Morillon as his bodyguard everywhere. He also sat in the back of all the meetings that took place and listened to what was being said, because he clearly could understand Serbo-Croat and until later on, by later on I mean about January/February and people started realizing that he actually could understand and hear of what was being said, it was very useful to have confirmation that the interpreters were interpreting correctly and that other things were not going on in the background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he later accompany you and General Morillon into the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was with us the entire time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did President Izetbegovic say to you at that meeting in early March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic said that a humanitarian disaster was in the making, that the Serbs were remorselessly attacking, that many people were being killed, that many atrocities were being reported and that the situation was very, very bad and could General Morillon personally go there to see for himself what the circumstances were, what was actually happening and, if the circumstances were as Izetbegovic had described them to be, to then make the necessary arrangements for humanitarian aid to be delivered, cease-fires to be arranged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He -- I just want to be absolutely clear about that. Did Izetbegovic have a specific clear request that a cease-fire be negotiated if possible, or facilitated I think is your word, if possible?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic's prime concern was for the well-being of the people and the refugees, and in order to ensure their welfare, a cease-fire was required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know of a place called Cerska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Cerska mentioned at this meeting in early March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. Cerska was the main area where President Izetbegovic was concerned about. Srebrenica was hardly mentioned. President Izetbegovic said that the situation in Cerska and Kamenica were dire and that he had had -- he, President Izetbegovic had had reports of atrocities being carried out against the Bosniak population by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you any idea as to what these reports were and from where they had emanated?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. He was not specific about any specific event or incident or time or place. He just said "atrocities" and what was the second part of your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where they emanated from? Did he give you any idea of who provided the reports?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. He did not give -- President Izetbegovic never talked about that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. What was the reaction of General Morillon to the request of President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon's response was to promise to President Izetbegovic that he would immediately try to go to Cerska and establish what -- what was going on there. What I need to -- need to explain is that up until that time, during February that is, the Lasva Valley had gone up in flames in the conflict between the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats and that General Morillon's focus of attention and the focus of attention of the Presidency had been on what was happening in the Lasva Valley. Now, in the background to this, there had been these, also these reports about Srebrenica, Kamenica, and so on. But they had been in the background. And President Izetbegovic's intervention swung the focus of balance for General Morillon and he had a clear request from the president, leave Lasva Valley, focus, please, on this. And so General Morillon promised, yes, that's what he would do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What precisely did he promise that he would do? What did he say that he would do?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He said that he would go as soon as he could to Cerska to see for himself what was happening and he did not say that -- he did not promise he would go there on any particular day, because it was difficult to move because of the constraints that the Bosnian Serbs put on -- on movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to get from Sarajevo to -- to the -- to Cerska, you had to cross enemy lines; correct? Sorry, warring lines, I should say. Lines of confrontation.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We would have to cross a number of confrontation lines to get to Cerska. Initially, we tried -- we planned, we tried to go by road from Pale up to Zvornik but the Bosnian Serbs refused and said that it was far too dangerous. We could not go that way. By good fortune, we had -- our headquarters had been working on helicopter corridors and we had just received, a couple of days previously, in Kiseljak, in the middle Bosnia, UN helicopters which for the first time had flown from Split down on the coast up into the middle of Bosnia. And General Morillon then said, we will try -- because it had not been done yet, it had not been proved possible, to fly by helicopter from Kiseljak to Tuzla and then cross the confrontation line between Tuzla and Zvornik and try to approach Cerska from the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could just interrupt you and halt you there, we'll get into the actual trip itself shortly. Did you actually leave for Srebrenica shortly after the meeting with Izetbegovic, in other words, a matter of days?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We left the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've agreed that lines of confrontation had to be crossed. And did you anticipate entering the Srebrenica enclave, the area held by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed that -- we had the meeting with President Izetbegovic, where he put the request. We then continued the meeting, but with Ganic, Dr. Ganic and General Sefer Halilovic, the Bosniak commander of the Bosniak armed forces and they discussed with us how we would get there and they said that they would notify their forces in the enclave, that General Morillon would be trying to approach them and that they would make sure that that information was passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember who said that to you, whether it was Ganic or Sefer Halilovic or both of them?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I can't remember which of the two it was, but -- but it was one of them. I can't remember which.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they present at the meeting when Izetbegovic made his request?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- obviously you spoke to them later. Who put you on to them? Who suggested that you speak to them or was it your own idea?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. It was President Izetbegovic who said, "Please now go and speak with Ganic and Halilovic, who will arrange -- help you arrange the details".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So President Izetbegovic made it clear that the details of getting into the Srebrenica enclave was something that they could facilitate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you go and speak to them and they tell you that they will notify their forces. Did they mention any names?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They mentioned Colonel Oric who was their commander, military commander in the pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they mention a Colonel or --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they give you the full name of this Colonel Oric or did they just say Colonel Oric? Or you can't recall? If you can't recall, say so.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say about him at this point? What did they say that he was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They didn't say anything special. There was no reason to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they mentioned the name -- they mentioned a Colonel Oric, who was a commander, and the military commander in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard of him up until that point?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. Naser Oric was first mentioned to us by the Bosnian Serb leadership in about the middle of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, okay. Well I will get back to that, what the Bosnian Serbs said about that later.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He had also been mentioned to us by our own intelligence people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will get into that later too. The Dr. Halilovic or Ganic ever explain to you how it was that they were going to notify Colonel Oric of your possible visit?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you set about making arrangements for your journey?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I was responsible for booking the helicopters, the clearances, for the team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were organizing it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people -- how big was your party when you eventually set off?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The party was, as we set off from Kiseljak, was General Morillon, Mihailov, myself, Larry Hollingsworth, from UNHCR. I think there was someone from ICRC, International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Do you know a fellow called Alan Abraham, Major Alan Abraham?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. He was a British major. He was the commander of the unit who we met in Tuzla, who provided us with the escorts and the military vehicles to -- when we went from Tuzla into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a ICRC representative who was with your party, a chap named Andreas Schiess?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Andreas Schiess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Schiess, I'm sorry, my apologies. And a doctor, Simon Mardell?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. He was a World Health Organisation doctor, who joined us in, I forget, it was either Kiseljak or Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to turn, before we get into the trip, just one -- the two topics that you've already just briefly mentioned. You said that the Serbs had mentioned Naser Oric to you prior to this occasion when Sefer Halilovic, or Ganic spoke to you in March. When had the Serbs spoken to you about Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They spoke to General Morillon --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Morillon.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: -- about Colonel Oric in Pale at a number of meetings we had there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it precisely who you are referring to when you say the Serbs spoke to General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We had one meeting with Lukic, another with General Gvero, and another with Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Lukic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Lukic was -- I think he called himself the prime minister of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you spoke to both political and military Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they say about Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They said that he was the Bosniak commander. They didn't use those words, they used the work Turk, "Turky" in Srebrenica, and they described him as the person who had led the attack on Kravica and who was leading terrorist attacks against Serb communities and who was, in their eyes, a war criminal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So they took that view of him. But did they ever explain to you why it was that they took that view of him, what sort of information they had that led them to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They said that the civilian population of Kravica had been massacred and that they -- the Bosnian Serbs -- had discovered a mass grave south of Zvornik in which they had - they, the Bosnian Serbs - had discovered about 50 killed Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if the Serb military commanders in their area had any equipment for intercepting radio messages?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I -- my staff tell me they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serb military or political leadership, during the course of these discussions that you've just been talking about, ever discuss intercepts with you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever discuss them in the context of Naser Oric? Intercepts, I mean.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Not at the meetings that we had in Pale, but when we were in Zvornik on the -- on the 5th -- on the 5th of March, on our way into Konjevic Polje, a Serb Colonel, Colonel Andric, he made a statement -- he said that they had just intercepted a communication between Halilovic and Oric in which Halilovic had told Oric that he was sending reinforcements to the enclave from a couple of locations north of Sarajevo, and that Oric had told Halilovic that he was going to continue with offensive operations, despite the arrival in the area of General Morillon or of an attempt by Morillon to go into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's an appropriate time for the afternoon break, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As -- or rather, in order to carry out your duties and assist General Morillon and for him to carry out his duties, did you require access to intelligence about the situation on the ground in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it was standard procedure for us to get an intelligence briefing, particularly about a new area that we had not been to previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the sources of those intelligence briefings? Who contributed the intelligence?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: These briefings were provided to us by our G2 intelligence staff, who were officers from -- intelligence officers from the UK, from France, from the Netherlands, from Denmark and the other countries contributing to the forces. The intelligence -- the information that they had came from a number of sources. It came firstly from reports which were submitted by the various battalions on the command of PH command. It came from reports provided by UNHCR. It came from reports provided sometimes by ICRC. It came from intelligence provided by the national governments of the contributing nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have briefings, intelligence briefings from time to time or only when you were going into a new area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. We had routine intelligence briefings once a week and then in any additional special circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any intelligence briefings about the Srebrenica enclave prior to going into the - into the area in March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we received an intelligence briefing in which we were told that the situation was understood to be bad; that we were told that there was fairly consistent fighting going on; that we were told that the Bosnian Serbs were under pressure because their line of communications between Zvornik and Pale were under continuous ambush. We were told that the Serbs were carrying on an offensive against the Srebrenica enclave. We didn't know precisely how far that offensive had gone. We were told that the military commander of the Bosniak forces in the Srebrenica enclave was Colonel Oric. We were told that there were reports that Colonel Oric had previously been a -- a JNA special forces soldier and that he had been a bodyguard of President Milosevic's. We were told a number of other rumours, but we had no way of judging their accuracy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- this information which you've just told us about, I assume that you and General Morillon had access to it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- we had a longer briefing than I just gave you in 30 seconds now, but, yes, we were both given this -- this briefing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thinking back now, can you recall when you received the briefing? Was it after the conversation with President Izetbegovic when he asked that you go to Srebrenica, but before you left? Or at some other time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. It was after we had our meeting with President Izetbegovic, because we went from Sarajevo, which is where we met with Izetbegovic, to Kiseljak and it was in Kiseljak that we received this briefing. We then, the next morning, flew from Kiseljak up north to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on into the area of the -- the topic of the actual -- your entry into the area of Srebrenica, I would like to just go back in time a bit. Did you meet a gentleman named Murat Efendic in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We met -- we being General Morillon and I -- met Murat Efendic a number of times in 1993 and it was mainly in February that we met. He was introduced to us by Zlatko Lagumdzija, who was the minister for refugee affairs, as being the representative in Sarajevo of the Srebrenica war committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you actually speak to Mr. Efendic, Mr. Murat Efendic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we spoke with him on at least two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever say anything to you that indicated he was not a member of the Srebrenica -- or representative of the Srebrenica War Presidency? Or did he confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: To be honest, I -- I cannot recall whether he explicitly said "I am a member of the Srebrenica War Presidency." That is the way he was introduced to us. Zlatko Lagumdzija requested that General Morillon meet with him and he was described by us as a member of the Srebrenica war committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did General Morillon, in fact, meet with him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the topics of conversation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was a plea from Murat Efendic on behalf of the people in Srebrenica to come to their assistance and a description by him of what the circumstances were that the people were having to live in in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he paint a pretty horrific picture of what was going on in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you spoke to him -- we know you told us you spoke to him in 1993, but did you speak to him prior to the meeting with Izetbegovic when he asked you to essentially to go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We met and I can't remember, it was either the end of January or beginning of February and then we met with him later on in February, but this was before -- before we met -- before President Izetbegovic's request which was at the beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us of your sources of intelligence. Did they give you an idea or a perception -- sorry, an idea of the general outline of the lines of confrontation in existence in early 1993? In that area, I'm talking about eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We had a belief of roughly what the confrontation lines were, which came, I believe, principally from intercept, radio intercept, but we did not have our own troops on the ground to confirm precisely where it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at this map that I produced to you. If Your Honours please, I would ask that the usher show the Defence the map first. You see on your screens, I think, a copy of the map that I hope to tender into evidence, but it is obviously -- will not include certain markings on it that I expect that this witness has put on the map. The reason for that is that was only created yesterday and there hasn't been time -- you can see the map is a large document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic are seeing now is what we have on the screen, you're telling us. MR. DI FAZIO: With markings on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. I understood that. MR. DI FAZIO: All I'm saying is I'm sorry I don't have 12 of them with the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. I mean that seems to be happening when -- there's difficulties. You can't avoid it, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Can I ask that the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will find a solution to it. MR. DI FAZIO: I would ask that you now look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now let's see this map. Is this what you were going to tender? MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I think if we used the ELMO, it's probably the -- and move the map around, it's probably the best way of doing it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
