utterances.text: We will see what -- how best to go about this. More or less we have an indication of where the markings are, and look like on that map. As we go along, I think the witness is already familiar with those markings. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'm going to ask him and I expect certain answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he is familiar with those markings, we can put the map on the ELMO, bit by bit as we go along. MR. DI FAZIO: That's what I meant sort of, move it around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand -- I understand the practical difficulties of making multiple copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At the same time, in order to take proper instructions from our client, we'll need at the court end of the court day, to have something which has those markings on it so we can follow to a certain extent what's being done on the ELMO, but we would ask either if we can borrow that copy of the map at the end of the court day or have a copy because, realistically, we can't actually seek instructions from our client when we met with him as to the confrontation lines et cetera. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. MR. DI FAZIO: I sympathise with their position. And I -- the Prosecution has no objection to the Defence taking -- using that particular exhibit, if the court's happy with that. On the undertaking, of course, that no markings be added to it. The usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It goes without saying. MR. DI FAZIO: Other than that, we're more than happy for the map to be provided so that they can get instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio and I am sure you will find a way between the two of you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, there is, I think, on the map, Colonel Tucker, you've got a little key explaining the various notations on the map. Just spread it out so we can see what is written there. Firstly, who made those markings on the map?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I drew the markings on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One's in black, it says "border". I think we can -- I can lead you on this, that that essentially follows the border between Bosnia and Serbia and in the eastern part along the -- much of the Drina River; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what does CFL represent?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The line in red with CFL is confrontation line and it represents, my understanding, and memory of roughly where the confrontation line was in early February --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, you referred to a -- a dotted line which is the symbol for line of communication and logistic resupply. Whose line of communication and logistic resupply are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is the Bosnian Serb army line of communication and logistic resupply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the remainder of the markings I think are self-evident. You circled significant towns and villages?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct, significant locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just pull the map up a little further. Thank you. You see that you have indicated a line of communication and logistics with the dotted line. Where does that go from and to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The dotted line goes from Zvornik here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: -- to Pale and around Sarajevo here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the significance of that particular line of communication, why was it important -- the logistics -- why was it important for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That road here is the only road which links this part of the Bosnian Serb held territory with this part of Bosnian Serb held territory. This road here, as you can see from the map, is very windy, but it is a passable road. However, from here, up to Zvornik, it's a mountain path. It's very twisty and it's a very difficult and dangerous road, particularly in winter, to pass. A much better road is from here through this route here, up to Zvornik in the south. That is a much safer road, a much faster road than this very difficult route here. From the Bosnian Serb perspective, they were very vulnerable here because you can effectively see that you've got the confrontation line and the pocket of around Srebrenica Cerska and Zepa here and you've got the Bosniak territory held here. This is a corridor, a gauntlet through which the Bosnian Serb army had to -- had to pass and their logistics had to go. I would also point out Han Pijesak, which is here, which was the headquarters of the Bosnian Serb army which was very close to the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just -- can you just point out where Cerska is, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Cerska is here. Kamenica is there. I would point out that there are about five places called Kamenica in eastern Bosnia. When I refer to Kamenica, this is the Kamenica at the time, referring to, which is south of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those two places assume military significance for the Bosnian Serb forces given your explanation about the line of supply and logistics?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. Because Cerska and Kamenica were on -- were bracketing this road here, which would have given them much better logistic communications through to Pale and their forces stationed around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Facilitated those lines of communication between Zvornik and Pale, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've -- we have both referred to something called the Srebrenica enclave. Just for the sake of completeness, can you please show the Srebrenica enclave to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Srebrenica is there. Zepa is there, Cerska is there. And this is what I refer to as the Srebrenica enclave. I would hasten to point out that this is not a formal front line in the way of traditional warfare. This is a very permeous line and it was very difficult to -- it would be wrong to think of it as a front line with -- with guards along all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Further south appears to be another area or enclave. What is that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: This area here is the Gorazde enclave. That is the town of Gorazde itself. I have marked dotted lines here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: -- and here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the significance?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: To signify that there was movement, or we understood, from the Presidency and from people who we met and from Murat Efendic, that there was movement between these two pockets and that there was also movement from Zepa up to Srebrenica and up to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I anticipate that you're going to give evidence that you went into Cerska in March, around the -- around early March. When you eventually did, did you find that Cerska had been taken by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived in Konjevic Polje on the 5th of March, we were met by Colonel Oric, who told us that we were too late and that Cerska had fallen a couple of days previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that -- just pull the map a bit further down. That's it, thank you. So what area of territory had they lost, had the Bosniaks lost from the enclave at about the time that you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: This had lost Kamenica a couple of weeks previously. They had lost Cerska two days previously. And the front line was on the high ground, to the north-west of this road here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. My eyes are -- can you actually see Konjevic Polje on that map?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. Konjevic Polje is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it marked? I can't see.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It is marked as Konjevici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that actually Konjevic Polje, though?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There are two Konjevic Poljes on the maps that I used at the time. There was a Konjevic Polje which was shown on the map as being just up in the hills, up here. I never went anywhere near that, that location. The Konjevic Polje which I referred to is the one which is at the junction between the road from Zvornik to Vlasnica and the road from Konjevic Polje through to Bratunac and Srebrenica, over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The road on that junction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I understand that this is not a precision military map, but does it represent broadly your understanding of the enclave areas and the lines of confrontation in February 1993, other than the qualification that you've just given about the chunk that was taken out following the fall of Kamenica and Cerska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. It's my understanding of what it was like roughly at the beginning of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any large difference that you understood in March --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: When we --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: When General Morillon and I went to Konjevic Polje, which is there (indicating), we were told that the front line was somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Between Cerska and Konjevic Polje. That was the 5th and 6th of March. When we arrived in Srebrenica on the evening of the 11th of March, we were told by the members of the Srebrenica war committee that Konjevic Polje was under attack by the Bosnian Serb army, that the British convoy which had gone there in order to evacuate the injured who we had discovered at Konjevic Polje, had been attacked by the Bosnian Serb army as well, and the next day we were told that Konjevic Polje had been captured by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In other words that the front -- this area had been taken and that this road here had been captured by the Serbs and the Serbs were able to use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's 511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so the map that Colonel Tucker has been using is being tendered -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're tendering this map. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I am Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. The map is being tendered and admitted into evidence and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P511. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already mentioned that you did in fact go into the enclave, the Srebrenica enclave. And that you went to Srebrenica itself. I want you now to focus on your initial contact with the enclave, which I think you've already said in evidence was around the 5th or 6th of March. How would you describe your basic purpose, that is General Morillon's and yours, purpose to -- in going there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon had promised to President Izetbegovic that he would go to Cerska to establish what the situation was and to do what he could, depending on what the situation was that he found, and that he would report -- he would return back to President Izetbegovic and tell him what he had found and done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Had President Izetbegovic complained of atrocities committed by Serb forces in the area of Cerska prior to your going there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic had said that atrocities had been reported in that -- in that area and it was one of reasons why he was so anxious and why he wanted General Morillon to go and establish what actually had happened, was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your travel on this occasion, did you go through Serb-held areas and speak to Serb commanders and Serb politicians?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We flew by helicopter to Tuzla and then joined a British escort who took us across the confrontation line at Kalesija and we then were taken to meet with Serb commanders and politicians in Zvornik, at the mayor's office in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they, in turn, complain to you of atrocities committed by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. The mayor of Zvornik complained about a mass grave which his forces -- of which the Serb forces had uncovered and were uncovering at that time. He showed us about a hundred photographs of partially decomposed bodies, which he claimed had been taken of those bodies, and that this was a war crime and that there were criminals in the enclave, in the Srebrenica pocket, and that whilst they were willing for women and children to be evacuated from the pockets, that no men were -- they would not allow any men to be evacuated because they had to check whether any of the war criminals who had committed these crimes were amongst them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How were you actually travelling into the Srebrenica enclave? How were you physically travelling towards the -- towards the end of your journey, towards the end of your trip when you finally crossed confrontation lines and entered the area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We had two small British armoured vehicles, a Spartan and Sultan. They're 8-ton, small armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you cross over into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We went south from Zvornik on the southern side of the Drina, to a little village which I think was call Drinjaca, something like that, and that was what the Serbs declared as being their front line. They then said there was a mine field between them and the Bosniaks and that it was our responsibility, if we chose to go into that mine field. We cleared our way by hand through the mine field and, in fact, drove over a mine which had been, I believe, deliberately placed there by the Serbs, but it didn't go off, fortunately. And we approached Konjevic Polje from the north, along this road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a map and I would like you to have a look at it and see if you can just -- if you can -- trace your route to Konjevic Polje. If the witness could be given a clear marking pen so that -- so that he may indicate on the map the approach into Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The location that the Serbs left us was about here on this map and we proceeded along the riverside, along this road here, which came around the corner here, until we met the outlying Bosniak forces who stopped us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm not going to ask you at this stage about all the details of the -- your encounter with the Bosniak forces. It's agreed, I think in this case, that you went on to Konjevic Polje. Can you just show the Trial Chamber the route that you took to continue eventually your journey into Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We carried on down this road here and this is Konjevic Polje here and that's the junction of the road carrying on to the south and that's the road going down towards Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area that you've marked, there's a place there called Konjevicvi. Further up you see Konjevic Polje. Now, where do you think you went?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Polje is Serbo-Croat for plain or flat area and this flat area here is what the map refers to as Konjevic Polje, which is the area. Now, the actual buildings that we went, where we met with Colonel Oric were near this junction here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours please, I tender the map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, Mr. Di Fazio. This map -- does it have an ERN number? MR. DI FAZIO: No, not that I can see. Would Your Honours like me to ask the witness to initial it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I am going to ask him myself. This map which has just been made use of is being tendered and received in evidence and this will be marked as Prosecution Exhibit number P512. Yes, Colonel, could you please initial -- put your initials at the beginning and at the end of the route that you have marked on the map, please. And sign the map either at the bottom of it or anywhere where it's ... Yes, that's fine. I thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thanks. Thank you. Now, let's get back to the journey itself. You have told us of the route you took. You eventually encountered some Bosniak soldiers you mentioned. Can you describe that event, please, and any difficulties that you may have encountered.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We had been moving slowly for about three kilometres, four kilometres, uncertain of where we would encounter the Bosniak front line and Mihailov, General Morillon's bodyguard, was carrying a United Nations flag and was shouting every hundred yards or so, we are the United Nations, hold your fire. At one point where I showed on the map that we met the Bosniak front line, somebody shouted down to us, down to Mihailov "stop". And after some shouting back and forth, a Bosniak soldier came down from the hill and we said that we had come to visit Cerska at the request of President Izetbegovic and could he please tell Colonel Oric that we had arrived and we would like to meet him and could he, the Bosniak soldier there, allow us to push out of the way the obstacle which was blocking our path. And this obstacle was a tree which was about two metres in diameter and about six, seven metres long, which was lying across the road. And our armoured vehicles could not get past, but the Bosniak soldier refused to let us -- he did not allow us to try and move the obstacle. There were also some mines around it and said that he could not let us move it until he had received permission from his officers. About an hour later, some officers came up who spoke with the Bosniak soldiers and gave us permission to move the tree. We then brought up the armoured vehicles with chains, they pushed and pulled and shoved and moved the tree out of the way, having moved the mines, the armoured vehicles moved past and they then pushed the tree back into place. We waited a further hour or so and then we heard the noise of cars without exhausts, very loud and two cars turned up with some of Colonel Oric's men. We were told to get into the cars. And General Morillon, myself, Mihailov and Larry Hollingsworth got into the cars and were taken in these cars from where the obstacle was to the school in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you to stop there. You said that two cars turned up and some of Colonel Oric's men. Did they announce themselves as Colonel Oric's men or was that your perception, your assumption?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was my assumption, because they took us to the school and it looked as if a couple of them were bodyguards and a couple of them were officers and -- because the officers joined in the meeting with Colonel Oric and Morillon in the school building, so therefore I assumed that they were Colonel Oric's officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So let's turn our attention to the school. The whole -- the party including armoured vehicles and all the men accompanying you also went to the school?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They followed about half an hour later, guided by Bosniak soldiers. So we went ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We, being you, General Morillon and the bodyguard Mihailov?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: And Larry Hollingsworth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And Larry Hollingsworth, okay. And what happened at the school?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: At the school, we were shown into a room by the people I described as Colonel Oric's officers and a short while later Colonel Oric arrived. By this time it was dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You hadn't met him up until that point?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I hadn't met him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He was dressed in combat uniform, dark -- dark green combat uniform, what I call winter uniform. But not white uniform. Not snow uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was interpreting for you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Mihailov was interpreting for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Colonel Oric -- sorry, let me withdraw that question. Did he introduce himself, Colonel Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say who he was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say he was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He said he was the commander of the Bosniak forces in eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you speak to him about or did he speak to you about?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We introduced ourselves and explained why we were there, which is at President Izetbegovic's request that we wished to establish what had happened in or what was going on in Cerska and that if it was necessary, that we wanted to establish a cease-fire, that we wanted to facilitate the evacuation of injured and casualties and that we wanted to negotiate the deployment of UN military observers in order to oversee the cease-fire and that we wanted to arrange for humanitarian aid to be delivered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he comment on these proposals or these notions, these ideas?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. He said that we were too late, that Cerska -- that Cerska had fallen two days previously and that we were welcome to try to go to Cerska but that the Serbs would never let us, because the Serbs had locked civilians inside houses and had burnt the houses and burnt the civilians inside the houses and that the Serbs would never let us near there because of these crimes that they had committed. He also said that there were about 700 injured in Konjevic Polje. By "in" what I mean is scattered in the various houses of the village because there was no large house or single location, who were unable, who were too badly injured to be moved on to Srebrenica. He said that the majority of the refugees had already, from Cerska and Kamenica had already passed through Konjevic Polje on their way to Srebrenica and that now there was only a trickle of refugees left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he comment on the cease-fire proposal or the cease-fire idea? I mean I know it wasn't a proposal but did he comment on the notion of looking at cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. He didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the time of this meeting, the approximate time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was in the evening, it was after dark. It was 8, 9 -- 8, 9 o'clock in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. And the date, the date of this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was the 5th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did your encounter with Mr. -- with Colonel Oric last?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he leave after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He went somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him again the next day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we saw him again the next morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll go into that in just a moment. Had you entered the enclave at the point at which you had expected to? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. We had entered the enclave at the point that the Serbs had allowed us to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in the vicinity of any area that you had expected to enter the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you provided any information to the Bosnian -- sorry, to the Bosnian Presidency or Mr. Halilovic or Mr. Ganic as to the approximate area that you intended to enter the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We radioed back to the British guard -- escort headquarters and asked them to inform Kiseljak to inform the Presidency to inform the Bosniak forces in the enclave of the route by which we were going to come into the -- approach the enclave and approach the front line, because we were concerned about not being shot as we approached their front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your expectation being what?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: This was the continuation of the conversation that we had had with Ganic and Halilovic on the 4th of March when they had said that they would ensure that their own forces were informed of the route that we were approaching, but they needed to know when it was and where it was. So I had to get the information back to them saying "We're coming in on the 5th and we're coming in from the north and we're coming in from Zvornik and we're coming in from Drinjaca" or whatever the name of that little village is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about what period of time elapsed between your coming across the tree trunk and the Bosniak soldiers and the appearance of Colonel Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was about two hours, three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next day, can you tell us how events unfolded.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The next day, we met in the morning, soon after daylight, and General Morillon said he was going to go to Cerska. Dr. Mardell was going to go around the village with a guide who was provided by Colonel Oric, to go and assess the casualties, the injured for evacuation, and Larry Hollingsworth went off to assess the situation with the refugees and we arranged to meet back at the school - I forget, at 12.00 or 1.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the result of Dr. Mardell's enquiries?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Dr. Mardell went round with a guide provided by Colonel Oric and he reported back to say that he had not found 700 casualties and injured, but 73.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you and Morillon do in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon had climbed into one of the British -- two British armoured vehicles and had driven off towards Cerska. I had been climbing into the back of this armoured vehicle when it suddenly drove off, and I fell out of the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: So the vehicle roared off, and because it had a high back the commander couldn't see I had fallen out of the back, so General Morillon went off into Cerska with me running behind the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And did he eventually make it into Cerska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw General Morillon when he came back from Cerska, he said that he had indeed gone up to Cerska, he had passed through the Bosniak front line. I had caught up to there on foot about half an hour later and waited there for two hours until General Morillon came back down. And General Morillon said that he had been to Cerska. He had come across a Serb sentry, a Bosnian Serb sentry, he had been very surprised to see him, who had introduced him to his Serb commander. There were about 30 Serb soldiers in Cerska who were what I would describe as professional combat soldiers, in other words not militia or home guard. And they had been courteous, polite and had just let General Morillon do what he wanted. General Morillon told me that he and his party got out of the armoured vehicle and walked around Cerska and looked at the damage and what had happened there. Other than a badly damaged village that had suffered, it had clearly suffered heavy fighting, he found no casualties or injured. Just these 30 or so Serb soldiers. He got back into the armoured vehicle and drove back down to the Bosniak front line, which is where I did climb into the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he report any bodies in houses that had been burned?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon said that he had, unfortunately - that he was unfortunately familiar with the smell of burnt human flesh and that he had walked around the village and that he had not smelt that smell and that he had not seen anything which indicated that anyone had been burnt or there had been people burnt inside houses. He said that he had not gone up into the woods and the hills around Cerska, so he had no idea of what was up there, but in the village itself, it did not seem, as far as he could see, that there had been anything other than heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you eventually make your way back to Konjevic Polje and the school?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. I got into the back of the armoured vehicle and we then drove the kilometre and a half, two kilometres back to the school in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Colonel Oric there at that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: And we met with Colonel Oric there and General Morillon told him that he had not been able to see any evidence, that he had been able to see, of people having been burnt in houses. Colonel Oric shrugged and said, "Well that's what my men told me." General Morillon also told Colonel Oric that Dr. Mardell had only found 73 injured and, again, Colonel Oric was not at all defensive or concerned. He just said "I never counted them myself. That's what I was told and I had no reason not to believe what my men were telling me".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your impression of Colonel Oric when you first met him? Can you comment on his bearing, his demeanour, his look, his age.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He was young. He was very intense. He looked very professional. He spoke clearly. He spoke in a measured manner. He was not emotional or histrionic. He gave every impression of being a professional soldier, in a very difficult situation, who was in strong command of his men and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you had a brief to discuss a number of topics and in fact did discuss a number of topics, including matters such as aid, cease-fires, and the atrocities committed in that area. Did he ever shrink from discussing those topics?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. He was very open. He was comfortable -- I had no impression that there was something he didn't want to discuss. The one impression I did have is that the thing which mattered most to him was that the Serbs were going to continue to attack, regardless of what General Morillon achieved or did not achieve, and that he was going to continue to defend in the best way he possibly could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would there have been any point at all in discussing a cease-fire with Colonel Oric had he not been commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I object to that question. That's -- would there have been any point at all in discussing a cease -- I don't know what sort of question that is, but it seems to be speculative and imprecise and has a lot of objectionable features, let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. I think you need to rephrase your question radically, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I will leave the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's very easy to put the same question in a different manner. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any intention of discussing cease-fires with persons who were not in the command, in the military command?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. We wished to discuss cease-fires with people who were able to make them happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- of the men accompanying Colonel Oric, did any of them introduce themselves to you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. None of them introduced themselves. It was very clear, from their behavior and body language and the way they talked amongst themselves, that they were subordinates and that Colonel Oric was the man in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you leave that day and go back to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We left and went back to Zvornik -- to Tuzla. Helicopters, back to Kiseljak and then by road into Sarajevo and reported back what we had seen and what we had experienced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reported to whom?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Reported to Izetbegovic and Ganic and Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And persons within your own command structure?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, along the way, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you reported to Izetbegovic, Ganic and Halilovic, did you inform them that you had spoken to the commander?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We informed them that we had spoken with Colonel Oric and we recounted to them what I've recounted to you here just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any -- did you detect any surprise when you spoke to them about Colonel Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The only surprise that we encountered was in Tuzla when we met briefly with the Bosniak commander of Tuzla airfields and he was very, very angry and vitriolic about the fact that General Morillon had refused to confirm that there had been atrocities in Cerska. When we reported the same to Izetbegovic, Ganic and Halilovic, they also expressed surprise that we had not discovered any clear evidence of -- of any atrocities, but were not nearly as emotional and histrionic as the Bosniak officers in Tuzla had been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already told us that, in fact, you returned to the enclave. When did you next enter the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We when we left the enclave, we told Colonel Oric that because we had now learnt that the situation in Konjevic Polje, other than for the 73 injured, there was not that much there but that the really serious situation was in Srebrenica and we told Colonel Oric -- or General Morillon told Colonel Oric that he was going to go back to Sarajevo to report to President Izetbegovic and he would then try to come back and go to Srebrenica, but he would come back with UN military observers and he would try to arrange for a cease-fire and he would try to arrange for humanitarian aid to be deployed and that he would arrange for the injured to be evacuated both from Srebrenica and for another convoy to go to Konjevic Polje to evacuate 73 injured who were in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you told Colonel Oric that you had now learnt that there was a really serious situation in Srebrenica. Who told you about that, who informed you of the seriousness of the developing situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Colonel Oric did. He said the serious situation is in Srebrenica now. It is no longer here. It has moved on. All the refugees, all those able to walk have all gone to Srebrenica. This is effectively a front line now. There's only going to be fighting here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he able to provide you with detail? Detail of the seriousness of the situation and how it was developing?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He gave us some numbers and I think he said something about 40,000 refugees in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He painted a grim picture?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that you told him that you were going to do all sorts of things, go back to Sarajevo, report to President Izetbegovic, come back with military observers, around a cease -- try and arrange a cease-fire, try and get humanitarian aid underway, evacuation of the injured. Did he react in any way to your proposals, Colonel Oric, I mean?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He was -- he seemed grateful that -- "thank you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So eventually you make your way back to Sarajevo, you said and you spoke to the President Izetbegovic, Halilovic and Ganic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And eventually you made your way back into Srebrenica. Did you request any forewarning -- a forewarning be conveyed to those within the Srebrenica enclave of your second arrival?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. This was normal routine. We asked Halilovic and Ganic to warn the -- warn their forces in the Srebrenica enclave that we were going to try and approach the enclave from the direction of Bratunac. And they said "Yes, we will get the message to our people".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say warned their forces. Who did you -- who do you mean by that? What precisely do you mean by "their forces"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The Bosniak forces in the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they -- did they agree to do that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They -- it was standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you arrive in Srebrenica again?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We arrived in Srebrenica -- not "again" because this was the first time in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In the town of Srebrenica on the evening -- it was again after dark -- of the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It was a very difficult trip, I think, to get into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs did everything they possibly could to obstruct us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about the main objectives of your previous trip to the enclave. What were the main objectives of this particular trip?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Now that we knew a lot more about the situation, we had specific proposals and intentions and General Morillon was accompanied by four UN military observers who he wished to deploy into the enclave in order to establish a cease-fire and he had issued instructions for further UN military observers to be redeployed from elsewhere in order to come and help man a cease-fire line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've also mentioned cease-fires. Was that one of the objectives of your trip to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. General Morillon specifically wanted to bring the fighting to a halt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned concerns about the injured in Srebrenica. Was that also an objective of your trip?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. Both injured in -- who we knew about, in Konjevic Polje, as well as, we had been told -- another thing Colonel Oric told us in Konjevic Polje was that there was one hospital in Srebrenica and Dr. Mardell had, in fact, left us and he went on foot from Konjevic Polje to Srebrenica while we wept back out. And so when we wept back into -- when we went into Srebrenica, we had a Medecins Sans Frontieres team of Medecins Sans Frontieres doctors with us in order to help with the injured in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you've also mentioned humanitarian aid in your evidence. Was that also a concern or objective --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- of this particular trip?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. There was a convoy of humanitarian aid stuck at Zvornik blocked by the Serbs and we wanted to get that convoy into Srebrenica. Because of a mistake by the -- by the Serbs, we managed to take one truck out of that convoy and turn it around and we were passing in the opposite direction, because we had been told we could only approach Bratunac on the Serb side of the river. So we had to go into Serbia proper. Now, the convoy was stuck trying to get the other direction into Bosnia. And as we passed the stuck convoy, we turned the truck around. It had medicine and sugar in it which we considered was the highest priority. And a Canadian armoured personnel carrier which is also stuck -- which is part of the Canadian battalion which had been trying to get into Bosnia for three months and was stuck there for three months, and they accompanied us to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the -- you've now given evidence of some of the objectives of the -- of your trip. Were they the principal objectives, namely, facilitation of the aid convoy, facilitation of cease-fires, deployment of UNMOs or military observers and evacuation of the injured. Is that a --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Those are the four objectives, though I would put them in a different order. I would put them in the order of deploy, UNMOs first, because you needed them to have a cease-fire and you needed the cease-fire in order to get the humanitarian aid through in order to evacuate the injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to achieve these objectives was it necessary for you and General Morillon to speak to a military commander in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just explain why, to the Trial Chamber, why that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In our experience, you only ever achieved anything if the military commander said "yes". If the local civilian commanders or mayors or whatever said anything, it didn't really matter. It was what the military commander said. And this was the same with the Bosniaks, the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Serbs, it was -- it was the way it works in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you stay when you arrived at Srebrenica, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We stayed in the new PTT building, which is immediately opposite the Srebrenica maternity hospital, which is the hospital I was mentioning a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stayed, I think, in Srebrenica for up until the end of March, around the 28th of March, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only hospital that you saw functioning in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just look at this photograph that I produce to you. This one. It's a partial photograph of a building. Partial photograph of a building. What building is that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That building is the new PTT building in Srebrenica, where we were accommodated on the top floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment before you say anything, Mr. Di Fazio. How shall we -- do we have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does this photo have a number already? MR. DI FAZIO: I think it's on the side there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a ERN number. What I'm -- MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether it has been tendered in evidence already, whether this is a new document that you are making use of? MR. DI FAZIO: It's a new photograph, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you want to tender this? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So this document is being tendered by the Prosecution as being marked 513?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. P513. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I think copies are coming, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: In essence, that's a post office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, postal and telephone. MR. DI FAZIO: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it being used as PTT at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were no telephone communications working by that stage. They had all been cut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what was it being used for, or as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was being used as the headquarters of the Srebrenica war committee, because it had a powerful radio in it with which they maintained contact with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Di Fazio, we have more -- MR. DI FAZIO: I will be tendering those other photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But would you require them to have different numbers or not? MR. DI FAZIO: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking you because ... MR. DI FAZIO: I will tender them at different times, if Your Honour please. So it's probably best if they have different numbers or would you prefer me to put them in as a bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I don't have a preference myself. But the thing is this, that this is definitely, I would imagine, a follow up to this and it says PTT building Srebrenica. It does have a ERN, which is one more than the previous document, but I don't know what you want to do with these photos. MR. DI FAZIO: We well I just wanted to tender the one photograph of the PTT building without any ERN numbers or second pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. Do you need this? MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honour, I do not need that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there are other photos. MR. DI FAZIO: I need just the photos, if Your Honours please, and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. For the time being, Madam Registrar, we're talking only of this document, which has become 513 and nothing else. So we'll keep these here and we will decide what to do with them later. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. We will be stopping for a break in 11 minutes time. MR. DI FAZIO: I think I can just deal with another topic in that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just advising you where we are time wise. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you have arrived and taken up residence, so to speak, in the PTT building. Did you meet any local officials, so to speak, on that night?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. As you can imagine, there was great excitement and within about an hour, hour and a half, we met with the -- a group of people who described themselves as being the Srebrenica war committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever met any of them before?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. Though one of them described himself as Murat Efendic's brother. Muret Efendic was the representative of the Srebrenica war committee who we had met in Sarajevo in February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members of this war committee turned up to speak to you or meet you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It's about eight or nine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They explained who they were?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of them explained who they were. One was called Hajrudin Avdic who described himself as the president of the Srebrenica war committee. There was another one called Nedjad Bektic, I'm sorry, my pronunciation is not good. There was another called --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will take you to names at a later point, but don't bother trying to recite them all. Did you meet them again in the ensuing days during your stay?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we met them on a large number of occasions over the following two, three weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where would you meet them when you met them over the ensuing weeks?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We met with them in a room on the first floor of the -- of the PTT building. It was the only room which had a, at that time, had a wood burning heater and it had a light bulb because there was a -- behind the PTT building there was a mountain stream and the Bosniaks had built a little water wheel which is linked to a generator producing a little bit of electricity and this electricity powered this light bulb. It powered the radios in the radio room and it was connected across the road to a couple of rooms in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you met with these members of the war committee, did you always meet them with the same group, all being present or did you meet different combinations of the group from time to time in meeting to meeting? In other words, sometimes all of them, sometimes some of them, sometimes singly?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We met with various groupings of them. However, Hajrudin Avdic was always there an he was the -- if Hajrudin Avdic was not there, we didn't have a meeting. He was the one who mattered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, during the course of these meetings, ever see Mr. Oric, Colonel Oric present?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the witness be shown Exhibit P510 and I think the witness has Exhibit P510 in front of him. Colonel Tucker, can I ask you to look at 3438, that's the ERN number. You can ignore the first four numbers and just go to -- it's like a page, page 3438 so to speak and also across the page into 39. Now, that's your handwriting, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is -- no, most of it is my handwriting. Not all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, there's an entry on page 3438, that says "Mesa" and what appears to be "brother of Murat Efendic". Can you explain that entry?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that Mesa was the name of the brother of the -- the first name of the brother of Murat Efendic who was on the war committee, a member of the Srebrenica war committee and another member of the war committee wrote the two lines which are above Mesa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if we can invite the assistance of the interpreters' booth, if Your Honours please. If that could be just placed on the ELMO briefly and we can see if it can be -- first of all, if it is legible and if it can be understood and we can get a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. You mean of the two lines above the word Mesa? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, the two scrawling lines that you can see and hopefully the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in case the interpreters -- MR. DI FAZIO: If they can read it, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking of those two lines in that box, the two lines above the line where you read the word "Mesa". MR. DI FAZIO: I think they're just conversing with each other.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter believes what it says is, "Your Goniba loves you very much." Goniba probably being a proper name. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, there we go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember now, Muret Efendic's brother wrote that in there for me to take back to him when I went back to Sarajevo. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much. I'm grateful to the interpreter's booth. Thank you, Ms. Usher. I am finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just turn over to page 3439. There are some entries there. They speak for themselves, their names, obviously, Hajrudin Avdic, Senad Alic, et cetera. Is that your writing?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. That -- what I did was I passed my -- this book here around the meeting and asked them to write themselves what the name was, because I was not good at understanding phonetically what they said and they wrote their names down. There was one person present at the meeting who described himself as a doctor. His name was Mujkanovic and he was at the far side and I wrote down his name, but he -- I didn't understand his first name and I then passed the book to him and he wrote Nadret as you can see on the document there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just turn back the page, back to 348 and there appears to be a date at the top of that page, 12 March, 1993, 15.15. I assume that means quarter past three in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 12th of March, correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is right. We had arrived in Srebrenica the previous evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And already met with this war committee?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is, in effect, is notes taken at a second meeting with the --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: At a third meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Third meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We had a meeting with them on the night that we arrived. We had a meeting with them in the morning. We then went around Srebrenica. We then had a meeting with them again back in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So all of these people were people who you understood to be members of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or sorry, let me be absolutely precise, what you call the war committee?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. I called it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, at the -- before the break, at the top, Hajrudin Avdic, there's some words there that aren't entirely clear, obviously president is one of them. Can you read out the remainder?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is my writing, "President of War COM" as in war committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, that is probably an appropriate moment. Would that be a suitable time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. We need to in any case. So let's have a 25-minute break starting from now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder as well as have having a quick look at the map, I wonder if it would be possible for us to just briefly inspect the diary during the break. I see my learned friend nodding, if that is okay? MR. DI FAZIO: I have no problem with it and I'm sure that Colonel Tucker ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You earlier testified that the hospital in Srebrenica was straight across the road from the PTT building. Did you have an opportunity to see people going in and out of the hospital, the weeks that you were there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We were straight opposite it and we saw the bodies being carried out in the morning and injured being taken in. We saw visitors going in. We saw people going out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have occasion to visit the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. I visited the hospital, in fact, on the first night that we were in Srebrenica and I visited again later on, during our time in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not in dispute in this case that conditions were pretty horrific in the hospital. Can you describe the conditions that you saw there and, in particular, can you comment on the state of exhaustion amongst the staff, the nurses and the doctors?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The conditions in that hospital were dreadful. The -- it was massively overcrowded. There was no lighting other than a couple of light bulbs that were powered from the little water-wheel generator. About 20 people a night were dying in the hospital, being buried the next morning. There was a pile of off cuts, pieces of human body, legs, arms, hands, fingers at the road side, opposite the PTT building which we only realized what it was later on when the snow started melting a little bit. There was one doctor in the hospital and a number of nurses and staff and their faces were the faces of people who had seen the inside of hell. They were shrunk. They were very, very tired. There was blood on their clothes. They were people at the very extreme of exhaustion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this spectacle that you were able to see inside the hospital, was it the same when you went again on the second Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. visit? In other words, that state of exhaustion that you saw and the shrunken faces of the doctors and the staff.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to show you a videoclip, please, from Exhibit P318.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop there, please. Do you recognise that fellow?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is the person I knew as Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, let's play on a bit. Just have a look.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The same person again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was his appearance when you saw him in the PTT building along with the other other members of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He was wearing combat clothing, beret, sunglasses, but did not look anything like the doctors or the staff who I had seen in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him go into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I never saw him go into or leave the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet him on occasions throughout the three or four week period that were you in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I met him on many occasions, almost always in the PTT building, which he hung around, and a couple of occasions in Srebrenica, walking in the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he have sunglasses when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he speak a little English?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to engage him in conversation, and found that he spoke some English. Because I didn't understand why, if he was a doctor, he wasn't in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your comments on that member of the War Presidency. And the other members of the War Presidency, you mentioned that you understood Hajrudin Avdic to be the main man within that war committee, as you call it. Did that perception ever change?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. He struck me as being the equivalent of the mayor of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the meetings that you had with the War Presidency, did you speak to them about the feasibility of a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We spoke with -- with him and the war -- the Srebrenica war committee on many occasions about a whole range of subjects, amongst them cease-fires and demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- tell the Trial Chamber if that topic of conversation, demilitarisation and a possible cease-fire, arose fairly early in your conversations with the war committee?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it arose about the third day, fourth day after we had established what was going on and other issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's not in dispute that there was a hostage situation, I'm going to develop that later. But at the moment I'm only concentrating on your encounters with the War Presidency and it's the topic of the cease-fire and demilitarisation I'm interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One matter to correct. There would be a dispute as to any hostage situation described that way. Just to alert my learned friend. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly I'm not suggesting that -- the evidence that I expect I will be leading, that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not taking it as -- if I went too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I think Mr. Jones is correct, but I have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. I think Mr. Jones is certainly right, but more or less I know where you stand, Mr. Di Fazio, on this. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Now, this topic of the cease-fire and demilitarisation, it arose and it arose about three or four days into your stay in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the War Presidency able to offer you anything constructive, in terms of -- starting about setting up a cease-fire? Or starting the process of bringing about a demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The war committee, whilst happy to talk about it, said that as far as demilitarisation was concerned, that they had opinions, but it was Colonel Oric that we needed to speak with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about cease-fires. Demilitarisation is one thing, a cease-fire is another. Did they offer any constructive comments with respect to that other matter of cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Similarly, they stated we really needed to speak -- they did not call him Colonel Oric. They just said Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. I would just like you to be absolutely clear. You started a sentence but I don't think you finished it. Similarly, they stated we really needed to speak ... and you didn't finish. Who to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: With Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. So your evidence is, you raised the topic. They were amenable to the idea, but said you have to speak to Mr. Oric about both topics, cease-fire and demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, one moment. Are these meetings with the members of the War Presidency of Srebrenica recorded in this diary or minuted in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them are. If I described the situation, we were, for a while, constrained inside the PTT building, could not leave the building and members of the war committee -- or various members came and went, so it was not clear. We now have a meeting, we now don't have a meeting. You're there. And you talk with people at various times. There were a couple of occasions specifically it when it was -- and in those cases it is minuted -- it is noted in the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am asking this question because you may have noticed me a little bit pensive just before the break. I've gone through this before in my career as a judge, as you can imagine. You have tendered a whole diary in evidence. And I am pretty sure, Mr. Di Fazio, that you will -- neither you nor Mr. Jones will be covering the entire diary. MR. DI FAZIO: You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in your examination-in-chief and cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honour is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would be very surprised if any -- either of you would try to convince me that by the time you are going through your examination-in-chief or your cross-examination, you have examined in detail each and every entry that there is. I wouldn't be surprised at all if in all truth there are parts that you can't even read because they are illegible, no offence meant to you, but your handwriting sometimes is atrocious. I am concerned, because basically what you have done is you have tendered this whole document in evidence. And once it is in evidence, it is in evidence. I wouldn't like the situation to remain as it is. I think if, in other words, you mean to have each and every entry that there is in this diary to constitute evidence in this case, you need to declare -- make such a declaration, because it's important. There may be things that may be relevant, things that may not be relevant, things that questions will be put on or about and things that will be overlooked. It's not the ideal situation. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, we then -- if we didn't do that we would be in a position where we're picking and extracting bits of the diary which may also not be ideal. On the other hand, we can't get this witness to go through and explain each an every entry because we'll be here forever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. MR. DI FAZIO: -- forever if we do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it assists, Your Honour, but as far as the diary is concerned, certainly my understanding is that it's been tendered as evidence, that it's the diary which was maintained by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But until he gives evidence about any of it, it's not in itself evidence that such happened. My plan was to take him to the passages which I would want his comments on and my understanding would be it would only be at that point we would have evidence, you know, properly understood. That's, as I said, that's my understanding and of course there may be other understandings possible, so it's a good thing Your Honour has raised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Jones. But in reality, it will be still constitute evidence as to its content at least. And what you have here remains here. This document will be examined by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It would be evidence that those entries were made but not that they reflect the truth of what they purport to record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying they reflect the truth of what they purport to show here, but there may be some damning evidence in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is -- MR. DI FAZIO: Does Your Honour wish the Prosecution to adopt a position as to whether or not you would later be entitled to look at any other entry that this witness does not comment on? Is that what's troubling the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like this. Our responsibility, as the trial judges in this case, is that if you have tendered this into evidence, it would be unsafe on our part to rely only on your questions and on the maybe couple of entries or a few entries that the witness is asked questions about and ignore the rest. We can't ignore the rest because the rest is here. MR. DI FAZIO: There is evidence of course, if Your Honours please, on the manner in which it was created and I can extract more evidence about that. Now, that will go some way to explaining the entries and the witness would -- I could ask the witness if he adopts the remainder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I put the question to the witness, the last question that I put to the witness on purpose, as you may have gathered. I asked him precisely whether he kept records of these meetings, when I say meetings, I'm using the word meetings in a loose form as indicated. And he said "yes". Now do you expect us not to try and find out what these entries are in this diary about these meetings even if you don't ask the witness any particular question on these -- on those entries? Of course we will. This is what we are trying to open your eyes at, Mr. Jones, in particular, and you also, Mr. Di Fazio, because I have been taught many years ago when I became a judge not to surprise the parties with anything. MR. DI FAZIO: Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think, I can't say more than I have stated, but you have got ample time to digest these words and you know, give us a lead as to what your intentions are when it comes to making use of this document as a piece of evidence in this case. MR. DI FAZIO: How you can treat it, in other words, and the contents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it is entire -- what you have submitted is an entire diary. I don't even need to say I agree with Mr. Jones when he says that its contents are not proof of the events, but in reality they are there. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes, I understand that. I mean it would be different when the witness comments in court of course about a particular entry. That's another matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's different. But the problem is more convoluted than that, I think. But anyway, let's move and then you have the whole evening and until tomorrow or even later to think about this and come back to us with some kind of. MR. DI FAZIO: Position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were talking about -- I was asking you some questions about meetings and you told us that you met with or encountered members in varying combinations of the war committee and that you discussed and spoke about cease-fires and demilitarisation over time with these members of the war committee. And I asked you -- I was starting to ask you if the War Presidency had provided you with any feedback as to the -- as to their attitude towards cease-fires and demilitarisation and I think your evidence was that they suggested that you speak to Naser Oric. My question is: Did you make an effort to contact Mr. Oric to do precisely as they suggested?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We kept asking the president of the war committee, please can you get in contact with Colonel Oric so that we can meet with him so that we can discuss these matters and they said, he is elsewhere and -- we are passing messages but we don't know when he's going to appear, we don't know when he's going to be here. And in the absence of Colonel Oric, we spoke with the people that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to ask you to turn your mind to another topic. If Your Honours please, we've got six minutes to go and this is a fairly big --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why six minutes to go? I think we have 20 minutes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, I was thinking of the earlier times. I apologise, if Your Honours please. So I think we do in fact have time to start the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't mind finishing. MR. DI FAZIO: I got confused momentarily, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you entered Srebrenica and took up your residence, so to speak, at the PTT building, could you see large numbers of refugees in and around that area, the hospital and the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, the place was thick with them. There were thousands of people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were there the following day on the 12th, as well?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. They had nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go up to the roof of the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: More often than I care to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about on that day, the 12th, did you go up there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you observe the crowd?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I went up and I went up for two reasons. I went up, firstly, in order to try and establish communications. We had an American tactical satellite radio. However, the satellite was 18 degrees above the horizon at right angles to the direction of the valley and only if we put a step ladder right on the edge of the top of the PTT building could we sometimes hit the satellite. It was just on the edge.
