The second reason for going up on to the roof of the PTT building was during the afternoon of the 12th, which is when -- shortly before we were prevented from leaving Srebrenica, I was already very concerned about our ability to leave Srebrenica and I was going up on to the roof because it was the best vantage point from which to see what was happening and the preparations which were being made to prevent us from leaving Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was causing your concern? What was worrying you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: When we had arrived the previous night, we had been welcomed. When we, the next morning, met with the Srebrenica War Presidency, the atmosphere had changed. Hajrudin Avdic was very uncomfortable and he wouldn't look us in the eyes and there was something wrong. And whenever we talked about right, we now -- we've seen what we need to see, we know what the situation is, we will leave the UN military observers here and the doctors here, we will go back to go and negotiate further UN military observers to come in. We were delayed and the war committee then persuaded us to go on a walk around the town in order to see -- but it was a delaying tactic. And the whole war committee walked around the town with us. It took about two hours, whatever. We then met again, the second meeting with the war committee, in the top of the PTT building on the first floor and it was a conversation that was going nowhere. It was clear they did not want us to go. And Morillon was arguing with Hajrudin Avdic. I went out of the meeting room to go and prepare our vehicles and whilst we were loading up the vehicles, Mihailov told me that, "Do you know what they're saying in the crowd?" And I said, "No." And he said, "They're discussing whether to kill you now or whether you served some use being kept alive." And I went back up on to the roof of the building, as I described earlier, and I saw some military preparations being made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Can I just interrupt you there. We'll get on to that in just a moment, the military preparations that you speak of. But what did -- can you recall anything specific that the members of the military committee said or did that made it clear to you that they didn't want you to go? Can you recall anything?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They said that the refugees were getting very anxious and that the refugees were very frightened and that if -- that when you, General Morillon, had left Konjevic Polje, as soon as you had left, the Serbs had started shelling Konjevic Polje and had attacked and they're afraid that if -- that if you leave now, that the same thing will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: By the way, my learned friend referred to the military committee. I take it he meant to refer to the war committee, just for the record. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, that's right. I'm sorry. Mr. Jones has corrected me properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you actually make an attempt to leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We mounted in our vehicles and tried to drive off and got ten metres before the crowd of refugees surged around us and laid down in front of the tracks of the armoured vehicle and blockaded us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is no way out except by running over these refugees?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That was not what we were there for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. So did you abandon the vehicles and go back in?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. We stayed with the vehicles and General Morillon climbed on top of the armoured vehicle together with Mihailov and tried to calm the refugees and tried to persuade them to let us pass, but to no avail. And eventually we had to reverse the vehicles, back up against the wall of the PTT building just by the entrance and we were manhandled upstairs to the first floor of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who manhandled you upstairs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Bosniak soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you earlier mentioned that you observed some military -- sorry, I don't want to misquote you, but you observed some preparations being made. What preparations were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There were two types of preparation being made. Firstly, a couple of heavy machine-guns, 12.7 millimetre machine-guns on tripods were being set up on a couple of positions which were overlooking the road down which we would have to go. Secondly, a barrier was set up through which -- or which we'd have to pass through in order to depart. Thirdly, some soldiers with anti-tank rocket launchers on their shoulders were by the sides of those barriers and, fourthly, there were soldiers who were moving and marshalling the refugees and organising the refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see this from?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I saw this from the first floor windows of the PTT building and from the roof of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw these prior to your going down and getting into the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct. And I went into the meeting which was still going on between General Morillon and the Srebrenica war committee and told him, "General, they're not going to let us go." And he said, "Don't worry, Pyers, of course they'll let us go" and they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many rocket launchers did you see, was it just the one?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was just the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how common rocket launchers were amongst the Bosniak military forces in the enclave, if you know, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I do. They're like gold dust. When I was at the Konjevic Polje -- when I was waving for General Morillon to come back from Cerska which is the road from Cerska, the Bosniak soldiers there had one of these rocket launchers and I was waiting there for two hours and talking with them and asked them how many of those do you have, and they said, Very, very few and we have to keep them for where we think the tanks will come. And I asked them where you get them from. They said we get them from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you discuss or mention or put to the members of the war committee these preparations that you'd seen, what you had seen, did you remonstrate with them or raise the topic with them?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it it's General Morillon's task to do that, no? MR. DI FAZIO: Indeed, I will develop that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Morillon raise these issues with them?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No, he didn't, because the war committee were portraying things as, this is a spontaneous protest by the -- by the women and by the refugees and later on they told us that the refugees had organised themselves into a women's committee and that it was the women's committee who were organising the refugees and they were powerless against these -- with this women's committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did the -- how did matters finish that day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Matters finished with us locked into the -- one of the big rooms on the first floor of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was locked in there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: All of our party, which was General Morillon, myself, Mihailov, Larry Hollingsworth, not the Medecins Sans Frontieres doctors, they were over in the hospital. There were two Belgian -- Belgian officer, driver, there were four United Nations, UN military observers. I have the list of the names in my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't have to have everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Locked from the inside or from the outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the outside. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about guards or sentries.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. With guards outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Armed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any idea or impression as to who these guards were or -- were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniform and they had weapons but in Bosnia that doesn't necessarily mean they're soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend the night under guard?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day was the 13th, I think.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any attempt, by General Morillon, to get himself out or extricate himself from that situation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. General Morillon tried to leave the pocket and he arranged with Mihailov and me that he would try to escape from the room and at about 10.00 in the evening he put on a big duffle coat and pulled the hood over his head, took his beret off, and when a number of Bosniak soldiers walked into the room, he walked out with them and they didn't notice that he'd gone. He went down the road which we'd come in to Srebrenica and went and stood in a house, a ruined house at the side, and I was supposed to try and leave the room early in the morning and take one of the Jeeps that we had and drive down past that building, pick him up and then head on down the road towards Bratunac, towards the Serb front lines where he hoped to cross the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you successful in slipping away in a Jeep, or not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. What happened is that I was escorted down to one of the Jeeps by some Muslim soldiers in order to use the radio, which was in the UNHCR Jeep, in order to radio back to our own headquarters what was happening and I asked him if I could move the Jeep to the side of the building because it was better communication reception there. He allowed me to do that. I then went back up into the room. At about 2.00 in the morning, by which time most of the sentries were asleep, most of the guards were asleep, I again asked can I use the radio and he let me go down and I got into the Jeep. I started the engine and as soon as I started the engine a lot of the -- the refugees were just scattered everywhere around, temperature was about minus 15, minus 20 degrees and the refugees were clustered around little fires. They were burning the plastic beer crates. The plastic beer crates, when you light them, they burn for about four or five hours and they give off quite a lot of heat. Actually they're little fires everywhere. The refugees woke up hearing the engine and then crowded around the vehicle and were quite angry and it was very clear to me that there is no way they were going to let me drive that vehicle anywhere. So I closed down the engine and went back into the -- went back into the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did -- I take it that the escape attempt failed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, obviously the escape attempt failed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did General Morillon do?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: About 6 o'clock in the morning, 7 o'clock in the morning, General Morillon came back into the building with his coat on and none of the -- none of the guards recognised him and he came back into the room. He was absolutely exhausted and he said that he had spent the night standing in this house, watching the refugees - it was snowing heavily - watching these refugees. It was these refugees who came from Cerska and Kamenica, and they had finally reached Srebrenica having gone on foot from up there and he had watched hundreds of these refugees slowly walking through the snow in the cold and he said, this is something I've never -- I've not experienced ever before. And that is when he made his mind up that he was not going to -- try to leave Srebrenica anymore and he was going to make a virtue out of the need and he was going to say "I am going to stay in Srebrenica". I put him in a sleeping bag and put him around the back of the room, another small side room, which -- it wasn't obvious there was a room there. The Bosniak soldiers came in for some reason looking for him and when they saw his sleeping bag empty they panicked and then they -- there was a lot of shouting and screaming and search parties were sent running off in all directions, but actually General Morillon was asleep in the back of the PTT building. And then at about 10 o'clock in the morning he woke up and then the war committee were in a panic by that stage and General Morillon shaved and just came out looking fresh as if nothing had happened and the war committee were absolutely so relieved. Then General Morillon said to them: "I'm going to stay". And things went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll just about wrap it up for today, but just one or two matters I wanted to establish. Did he eventually give a speech to the assembled refugees and people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, he gave a speech from the first floor of the PTT building that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That afternoon, right. And did you work with him on preparing the text of that speech?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We spent the morning working out what he would say and the speech is in this and the speech was read out of this notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours please, I'm not finished with the topic but this is a natural break for -- in the midst of the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. We'll meet again tomorrow in the afternoon, same courtroom, courtroom 2 at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of March, 2005 at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.55 p.m., to
